It also costs you more than the three lines it takes up, because Cliffy infers the option and argument types only inside the handler. Move the work out and you end up hand-writing a ListFlags interface that restates your .option calls, and now the two can drift apart. Put the implementation in the handler and all of that goes away. ruleCards.rationale: Ported from dmmulroy/anti-slop , which builds it on padding-line-between-statements from ESLint Stylistic. Generated code often packs imports, declarations, and control flow into one block of text. This rule requires a blank line after imports and between top-level statements. It also requires one around functions, classes, interfaces, types, and bindings that span lines. Control flow gets one before it, and a statement that ends in a block gets one after it. Runs of one-line bindings stay grouped, and so do imports and overloads. A binding with its own comment starts a new group. The fix adds blank lines and never removes them. With no options, the rule follows anti-slop. Spacing is a matter of taste, so every part of that policy can change. Each requirement has its own switch: afterImports: a blank line after the import group. betweenTopLevelStatements: blank lines between top-level statements. aroundDeclarations: blank lines around functions, classes, interfaces, and types. aroundMultilineBindings: blank lines around const, let, and var that span lines. beforeControlFlow: a blank line before if, loops, switch, try, and return. afterBlocks: a blank line after a statement that ends in a block, such as an if or a function. The allow switches, off by default, keep related statements together: allowAttachedUses: below module scope, a statement may follow a one-line statement with no blank line when it reads a name that statement declares or assigns. That covers const ready = await check(path); followed by if (ready) {, let result = ""; before the loop that builds result, and index = next(index); before if (index === -1) return;. allowGuardClauseRuns: one-line if statements stay grouped, and so does a one-line return or throw right after one. A multi-line if still needs a blank line after it. allowMultilineBindingRuns: consecutive bindings stay grouped even when one of them spans lines. A binding with its own comment still starts a new group. For anything the switches don't cover, overrides takes entries shaped like ESLint Stylistic's: { blankLine, previous, next }. The rule checks them in order, before anything built in, and the first entry that matches a pair of adjacent statements decides it. blankLine: "always" requires a blank line and blankLine: "any" accepts either spacing. previous and next each take one statement kind or a list of them. Add usesPrevious: true to match only when the second statement reads a name the first one declares or assigns. For example, this keeps a one-line binding next to the function below it: { blankLine: "any", previous: "single-line-binding", next: "function" }. Turn every requirement switch off and overrides becomes a policy of your own. The statement kinds are: *: any statement. binding, single-line-binding, multiline-binding: const, let, var, and using declarations. declaration, function, class, interface, type, enum, overload: declarations, where overload is a function signature with no body. import, export, and top-level, which excludes imports. expression: a call, an assignment, or another expression on its own. control-flow, if, single-line-if, loop, switch, try, return, throw, break, continue: control flow, where control-flow covers if, loops, switch, try, and return. block-like: a statement that ends in a block, such as an if, a function, or const f = () => {};. single-line, multiline: any statement, by whether it fits on one line. Declaration and binding kinds match through export and export default, so function matches export function detect() {} too. This port differs from anti-slop in a few ways: All the options are local, since upstream has none. It matches functions, classes, interfaces, types, and bindings by node type, so abstract, declare, and decorated forms count too. Exported bindings count as bindings, including multi-line ones. It checks export = value like any other statement. Upstream skips it. It keeps only the parts of ESLint Stylistic's engine that this rule uses. The rule never removes blank lines.

ruleCards.description: Enforce that React hooks are only called at the top level of components or custom hooks, never conditionally or in nested functions
messages: This hook is being called after an early return. Hooks must be called unconditionally and in the same order every render.
This hook is being called conditionally. All hooks must be called in the exact same order in every component render.
This hook is being called from a nested function. All hooks must be called unconditionally from the top-level component.
This hook is being called inside a loop. All hooks must be called in the exact same order in every component render.
This hook is being called inside a try block. Hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level.
This hook is being called recursively. Recursive calls require a condition to terminate, which violates hook rules.
